# The Kérberos file: from cerberus to the temple it became
Some restorations are cosmetic. **Kérberos** is not — the marks in this name are the difference between reading the sources and guessing at them.

Kérberos' myths are the myths of every threshold that must not be crossed — and of the handful of heroes who crossed his anyway. Hesiod sets him in the monstrous brood of Typhon and Echidna (Theogony 306-312): Orthrus the hound of Geryon, then "Cerberus the flesh-eater, the brazen-voiced hound of Hades, fifty-headed, shameless and strong," and after him the Lernaean Hydra and the Chimaira.  The family is the underworld's kennel and armory in one: wherever the myths need an impossible guardian, one of Echidna's children is already on duty.

That is the figure this file is about — and the temple now standing at its restored name.
## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Kérberos
- **ASCII form:** cerberus
- **Meaning:** "Spot, darkness"
- **Domain of influence:** Underworld Guardian
- **Pantheon:** Greek
- **Classification:** Tier 2
- **Original script:** Κέρβερος
- **Series:** The Restoration Files, No. 54 of 271
## The Name Before the Marks

The name is attested as **Κέρβερος**. On the evidence, it means "Spot, darkness".

Strip **Kérberos** to *cerberus* and one piece of evidence vanishes:

- **e → é** — Acute on e: the stress position the ASCII form cannot show.

A reader who knows the marks hears the name correctly on the first try. A reader who never sees them never gets the chance.
## The Temple That Stands Now

The restored name is not a plaque; it is an address. The temple of **Kérberos** lives at [/sites/cerberus/](/sites/cerberus/), with its mythology in the [lore halls](/sites/cerberus/lore/), its peer-reviewed record in the [Scholarly Edition](/sites/cerberus/scholars/), and its place in the pattern atlas on the [patterns floor](/sites/cerberus/patterns/).

The restoration preserves one decisive feature the ASCII form drops — a single, honest mark — which places it in Tier-2: exact, and exactly labeled.

Every flagship temple is hand-built to the same standard: the original script displayed with its provenance, the pronunciation reconstructed phoneme by phoneme, the sources named — because a restoration you cannot audit is just a spelling with confidence.
## The Archetype at Work

A temple is also a reading of what this figure *means* — and meanings have addresses in the modern world. The [pattern atlas](/patterns/) maps **Kérberos** to the industries its archetype genuinely resonates with, each match argued, weighted, and open to challenge:

- **Cybersecurity & Digital Protection** — The three-headed watchdog at the gate; the perimeter that never sleeps.
- **Defense, Military & Security** — The warden of the dead; border security with three heads and one rule — none leave.
- **Pet Care & Animal Industries** — The most famous hound in myth; the ancestor of every guard dog.

The mapping is conservative on purpose: only resonances that can be argued aloud. The rest of the atlas follows the same rule, industry by industry.
## In the Sacred Texts

The Greek tradition is not a vibe; it is a library. The [Sacred Texts collection](/texts/) holds [Theogony](/texts/theogony/), [Homeric Hymns](/texts/homeric-hymns/), and [Works and Days](/texts/works-and-days/) — the primary sources the temple's scholarship is built on, free to read, cross-linked back to the names they mention. The temple is the argument; the texts are the evidence.
## The File Continues

This is one of 271 Restoration Files — a second dispatch from every flagship temple in the fleet. The temple's [first dispatch](/sites/cerberus/blog/) tells the founding story of the name; the [blog index](/blog/) holds the whole archive.

Continue the series — previous file: **Qāyīn** ([read it here](/sites/cain/blog/restoration/)) · next file: **Cerēs** ([read it here](/sites/ceres/blog/restoration/)).

*The Restoration Files are written from the same canonical record as the temples themselves: the lexicon, the lore catalog, the pattern atlas, and the cited scholarly sources. If a file ever disagrees with its temple, the temple is right — tell us, and the file will be corrected.*
